Paper: Ho, Jain, and Abbeel (2020), [Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239).
A DDPM learns to reverse a fixed sequence of small corruptions, turning Gaussian noise into a sample through a sequence of learned denoising transitions.
Its practical training objective predicts the noise added to a data example.

## Problem

A complex data distribution is difficult to sample directly, whereas a Gaussian is easy to sample.
Diffusion modelling connects the two through a forward process that progressively destroys structure and a learned reverse process that reconstructs it.
Here $x_0$ is a clean data example, $x_t$ is its noisy state, and $t$ indexes corruption strength rather than physical time. [Paper, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=2).

## Previous attempts

Earlier diffusion probabilistic models already used a forward corruption chain and a learned reverse chain.
Denoising score matching learned directions related to noisy-data log-density gradients.
This paper connects those approaches through a particular reverse-mean parameterisation and a reweighted variational training objective that improves sample quality in its experiments. [Paper, §§1–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=1).

## Proposed solution

Choose variances $\beta_t\in(0,1)$ and define

$$
  \alpha_t=1-\beta_t,
  \qquad\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s.
$$

The fixed forward transition is

$$
  q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})
  =\mathcal N(\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1},\beta_t I).
$$

The standard deviation of the added noise is $\sqrt{\beta_t}$.
At any selected timestep, a noisy example can be sampled directly:

$$
  x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0
  +\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,
  \quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
$$

Thus $q(x_t\mid x_0)$ has covariance $(1-\bar\alpha_t)I$, not $(1-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t})I$.
When $\bar\alpha_T$ is sufficiently small, the terminal distribution is approximately standard Gaussian for the intended data scaling. [Paper, Eqs. (2) and (4)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=2).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: accumulate independent noise variances"}

Let each transition use an independent $\epsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$.
Unrolling two steps gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  x_2={}&\sqrt{\alpha_2\alpha_1}x_0\\
  &+\sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}\,\epsilon_1
  +\sqrt{\beta_2}\,\epsilon_2.
  \end{aligned}
$$

The two noise terms have combined covariance

$$
  (\alpha_2\beta_1+\beta_2)I
  =(1-\alpha_2\alpha_1)I.
$$

In general, if $v_{t-1}=1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$, then

$$
  v_t=\alpha_t v_{t-1}+\beta_t
  =1-\bar\alpha_t.
$$

This induction gives the closed-form corruption distribution.
Independent Gaussian variances add; their standard deviations do not simply add.
For example, two independent additive noises of variance $\beta$ produce variance $2\beta$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{2\beta}$.

:::

The learned reverse process starts from $p(x_T)=\mathcal N(0,I)$ and uses transitions

$$
  p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
  =\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(x_t,t),\sigma_t^2I).
$$

The original paper fixes the reverse variance in its main parameterisation and learns the mean through a noise-prediction network:

$$
  \mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}
  \left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}
  {\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\right).
$$

The network receives the noisy sample and the timestep, and its output has the same shape as the sampled noise target. [Paper, §3.2, Eq. (11)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=4).

## Why noise prediction is a variational objective

Treating $x_1,\ldots,x_T$ as latent variables gives an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood.
The bound separates a terminal-prior term, reverse-transition KL terms, and a reconstruction term at the final denoising step. [Paper, Eqs. (3) and (5)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=2).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: decompose the negative ELBO"}

Let $X=x_{1:T}$ denote the whole latent chain.
For a fixed clean example, Jensen's inequality gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  -\log p_\theta(x_0)&\leq L(x_0),\\
  L(x_0)&=\mathbb E_{q(X\mid x_0)}
  \left[\log\frac{q(X\mid x_0)}{p_\theta(x_0,X)}\right].
  \end{aligned}
$$

Factor the forward chain in reverse order while conditioning on $x_0$:

$$
  q(X\mid x_0)=q(x_T\mid x_0)
  \prod_{t=2}^{T}q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0).
$$

Substituting the reverse-model factorisation yields

$$
  L=\mathbb E_q\left[L_T+
  \sum_{t=2}^{T}L_{t-1}+L_0\right],
$$

$$
  L_T=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\Vert p(x_T)),
$$

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  L_{t-1}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(&q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\\
  &\Vert p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\big),
  \end{aligned}
$$

$$
  L_0=-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1).
$$

With a fixed forward schedule and terminal prior, $L_T$ has no learned parameters.
The final reconstruction term $L_0$ still depends on the model and must not be discarded as a constant.
For discrete image pixels, the paper defines it using a discretised decoder likelihood. [Paper, §3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=4).

:::

The posterior $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ is tractable because it conditions on the original clean example.
This is a training target; a reverse sampler cannot condition on the unknown clean answer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: Gaussian posterior and the weighted noise loss"}

For $t\geq2$, multiplying the two Gaussian factors in

$$
  q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)
  \propto q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)
$$

gives a Gaussian with variance and mean

$$
  \tilde\beta_t
  =\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\beta_t,
$$

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \tilde\mu_t={}&
  \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}
  {1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0\\
  &+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}
  {1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t.
  \end{aligned}
$$

The first coefficient includes $\beta_t$.
For a reverse variance $\sigma_t^2$ fixed independently of $\theta$, the KL becomes

$$
  L_{t-1}=\frac{\|\tilde\mu_t-\mu_\theta\|^2}
  {2\sigma_t^2}+C_t,
$$

where $C_t$ is independent of $\theta$.
If the two variances differ, the variance contribution remains part of that constant; the KL is not exactly just the mean error.
Substitute the direct corruption formula to express the posterior mean using its sampled noise, then use the learned noise parameterisation:

$$
  L_{t-1}=w_t
  \|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2+C_t,
$$

$$
  w_t=\frac{\beta_t^2}
  {2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}.
$$

This is the timestep-weighted noise error obtained from the variational bound. [Paper, Eqs. (6)–(12)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=3).

:::

The practical simplified objective removes that timestep weighting:

$$
  L_{\mathrm{simple}}
  =\mathbb E_{t,x_0,\epsilon}
  \|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2.
$$

Here $t$ is sampled uniformly from the training timesteps.
This reweights the learning problem; it is not an algebraically identical name for the original weighted variational bound. [Paper, §3.4, Eq. (14)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=5).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Implementation: train on one directly sampled corruption"}

This minimal fragment illustrates the objective without prescribing a particular denoiser architecture.

```python
t = torch.randint(1, T + 1, (x0.shape[0],), device=x0.device)
eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
shape = (-1,) + (1,) * (x0.ndim - 1)
a_bar = alpha_bar[t].reshape(shape)
xt = a_bar.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - a_bar).sqrt() * eps
eps_hat = denoiser(xt, t)
loss = (eps_hat - eps).square().flatten(1).mean(1).mean()
```

The timestep conditions the network because the same noisy values can require different predictions at different corruption strengths.
An image U-Net can inject a timestep embedding into its blocks and use skip connections to preserve spatial information.
Training uses MSE against the sampled noise and does not require unrolling the reverse sampling chain for every minibatch. [Paper, Algorithms 1–2 and §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=4).

:::

## Evidence

The paper reports image-generation experiments on CIFAR-10 and LSUN, including ablations over parameterisations and training objectives.
These results support the noise-prediction parameterisation and simplified objective for the tested image models. [Paper, §4 and Table 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239#page=5).

## Limitations

Original DDPM generation requires repeated network evaluations and ordinarily samples fresh reverse-transition noise, except at the final step.
The approximate terminal Gaussian, learned reverse transitions, and numerical sampling choices all affect the generated distribution.
The theoretical forward posterior is available during training because $x_0$ is known; it is not an oracle accessible at inference.
